newsitem.title: UK: UK minutes show BOE may want half point rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK minutes show BOE may want half point rate rise.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George told Chancellor Kenneth Clarke at their December 11 monetary meeting that interest rates would probably need to rise by half a percentage point in the next few months.

"To keep ahead of the game, the Bank would advise an immediate quarter percent move this month. Although the Bank could not claim that it was crucial to move again now, if rates were not raised this month, it was quite likely on the information that was already available that the Bank would need to advise a half percent move in either January or February," the minutes quoted George as saying.
George said that on a two-year view, the Bank still thought the odds were that RPIX inflation would be above the government's target of 2.5 percent, and risks were on the upside.

Clarke said the case had not been made for a further rise in interest rates in December. "The difference between himself and the Governor was on the pace of policy tightening," the minutes said. "Overall, the Chancellor thought the picture was still mixed, with the indicators giving differing signals."

"While many of the indicators pointed to accelerating activity, there were some notable exceptions, in particular, the early indication of a slowdown in retail sales for November, the fall in car registrations and the continuing fall in producer prices," the minutes said.

Clarke said that given the strength of the exchange rate and weak commodity prices, low producer price inflation was not surprising. "The exchange rate could be expected to reduce these pressures further," he said. He added the data showed healthy growth in the economy but this was in line with expectations and the pace was not speeding up.
Clarke noted that underlying inflation had risen over the previous month to over 3.0 percent.

"He expected it to stay close to that rate for some months, given the profile of the index a year before. But this underlined the fact that the retail prices index was essentially a backward looking indicator. Whether inflation fell back to 2.5 percent in the first part of next year depended on policy decisions taken 12 to 18 months before," the minutes said.
